title: Angiosperms and Economic Botany

toc.title: 5.1 Morphology of root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower and fruit
5.3 Economic importance of plant groups in Nepal
5.4 Medicinal plants of Nepal: neem, sarpagandha, yarsagumba, tulasi and ginger

html:
Angiosperms and economic botany close the Biodiversity unit and carry about 3 of the 40 Botany questions — the most of any Biodiversity chapter.

The questions come from four places: plant morphology (which organ a potato, an onion or a pea tendril really is; inflorescence, placentation, fruit types); the four prescribed families (read a floral formula, name the family, give its fruit); the economic importance of every plant group in Nepal; and the five medicinal plants covered in this unit — neem, sarpagandha, yarsagumba, tulasi and ginger — with their scientific names, parts used and active compounds.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Modified organs by origin — potato, ginger, onion, Colocasia (stems); sweet potato, carrot, radish (roots); pea tendril, Opuntia spine (leaves); Opuntia pad, Asparagus "leaf", Citrus thorn (stems).
  • Inflorescence — racemose (acropetal) vs cymose (basipetal); special types: verticillaster (tulasi), cyathium (Euphorbia), hypanthodium (fig), capitulum (sunflower).
  • Flower terms — symmetry, ovary position, aestivation, cohesion of stamens (monadelphous, diadelphous, syngenesious), tetradynamous and didynamous, placentation.
  • Fruits — simple, aggregate, composite; true and false; legume, siliqua, berry, capsule, pome.
  • Four families — Brassicaceae K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G₍₂₎; Fabaceae K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G₁; Solanaceae K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎; Liliaceae P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎ — with one diagnostic character each.
  • Economic botany of Nepal — biofertilisers, fermented foods (gundruk, kinema), antibiotics, lokta paper, sal timber, pine resin, invasive weeds.
  • Medicinal plants — Azadirachta indica, Rauwolfia serpentina, Ophiocordyceps sinensis, Ocimum sanctum, Zingiber officinale.

5.1 Morphology of root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower and fruit

Root

The tap root system grows from the radicle (dicots); the fibrous root system of monocots replaces the short-lived primary root with many roots from the base of the stem; adventitious roots arise from any part other than the radicle.

Modification Function Examples
Conical / fusiform / napiform tap roots storage carrot / radish / turnip and beet
Tuberous (adventitious) root storage sweet potato
Fasciculated roots storage Dahlia, Asparagus
Prop roots (from branches) support banyan (Ficus benghalensis)
Stilt roots (from lower nodes) support maize, sugarcane, Pandanus
Climbing roots climbing betel, money plant (Pothos)
Pneumatophores (negatively geotropic) breathing in swamps mangroves — Rhizophora, Avicennia
Velamen roots absorbing moisture from air epiphytic orchids (Vanda)
Haustoria (sucking roots) parasitism dodder (Cuscuta, total stem parasite); mistletoes (Loranthus, Viscum, partial)
Root nodules nitrogen fixation legumes (Rhizobium); alder, uttis (Frankia)

Stem

The stem bears nodes, internodes and buds, grows towards light, and in its modified forms can always be recognised by these — a structure with nodes, buds or scale leaves is a stem, however root-like it looks.

Modification Recognise it by Examples
Rhizome horizontal underground stem with nodes, scale leaves, buds ginger, turmeric, banana
Stem tuber swollen tip of an underground branch; "eyes" are nodes with buds potato
Corm short, upright, swollen underground stem Colocasia (pindalu), Amorphophallus, Crocus, Gladiolus
Bulb reduced disc-like stem with fleshy scale leaves onion (tunicated), garlic (compound bulb of cloves), lily (scaly)
Runner, stolon, offset, sucker sub-aerial branches that root and form new plants Cynodon (dubo grass), strawberry (runners); jasmine, mint (stolons); Pistia, water hyacinth (offsets); Chrysanthemum, banana, pineapple (suckers)
Stem tendril from an axillary or terminal bud grape vine, cucurbits
Thorn from an axillary bud; has vascular supply Citrus, Bougainvillea, pomegranate
Phylloclade flattened green stem of many internodes; leaves reduced to spines Opuntia, Euphorbia
Cladode green stem only one internode long Asparagus, Ruscus
Bulbil fleshy axillary bud that drops and grows Dioscorea, Agave
Thorn, spine and prickle

A thorn is a modified stem (axillary branch — Citrus, Bougainvillea). A spine is a modified leaf or part of a leaf (Opuntia, Berberis; stipular spines of Zizyphus).

A prickle is only an epidermal outgrowth with no vascular tissue (rose). Thorn and spine have the same function but different origins — they are analogous.

Leaf

A leaf has a leaf base (swollen into a pulvinus in legumes, sheathing in grasses), a petiole and a lamina; many have a pair of stipules.

  • Venation: reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots (exceptions: Smilax and Dioscorea are monocots with reticulate venation; Calophyllum is a dicot with parallel venation).
  • Compound leaves: pinnate — leaflets on a rachis (neem and rose, imparipinnate; tamarind, paripinnate; Mimosa, bipinnate; Moringa, tripinnate); palmate — leaflets from one point (unifoliate Citrus, trifoliate Aegle (bel) and Oxalis, quadrifoliate Marsilea, multifoliate silk cotton, simal). A compound leaf has a bud in its axil; a leaflet has none.
  • Phyllotaxy: alternate (one leaf per node — mustard, China rose), opposite (two per node — guava, Calotropis (decussate)), whorled (more than two — Alstonia (chhatiwan), Nerium).
Leaf modification Examples
Leaf tendril pea (terminal leaflets); Lathyrus aphaca (whole leaf; the stipules become leaf-like)
Leaf spines Opuntia, cacti, Berberis
Phyllode (flattened green petiole) Australian Acacia
Pitcher / bladder (insect traps) Nepenthes / Utricularia
Fleshy storage leaves onion bulb scales, Aloe
Heterophylly (different leaves on one plant) Sagittaria, Ranunculus aquatilis, Limnophila

Inflorescence

Feature Racemose (indefinite) Cymose (definite)
Main axis grows on indefinitely ends in a flower
Order of flowers acropetal — oldest at the base, youngest at the tip basipetal — oldest at the tip
Opening centripetal (outside → in) centrifugal (inside → out)
Racemose type Character Examples
Raceme long axis, pedicellate flowers mustard, radish
Spike long axis, sessile flowers Achyranthes, Amaranthus
Spikelet small spikes with glumes wheat, rice (grasses)
Catkin pendulous spike of unisexual flowers mulberry, willow, birch
Spadix fleshy axis enclosed by a large bract, the spathe Colocasia, banana, maize (female)
Corymb lower pedicels longer, flowers at one level candytuft (Iberis)
Umbel pedicels from one point, with an involucre of bracts coriander, carrot (compound umbel), Centella
Capitulum (head) flat receptacle with sessile ray and disc florets, involucre sunflower, marigold, Tridax

Cymose types: monochasial (one branch below the terminal flower — helicoid or scorpioid), dichasial (two — jasmine), polychasial (several — Calotropis).

Special types: cyathium (a cup of bracts with one female flower surrounded by male flowers — Euphorbia, poinsettia); verticillaster (a pair of cymes at each node, looking like a whorl — tulasi, Leucas, Lamiaceae); hypanthodium (a hollow, flask-shaped receptacle with flowers inside and a small pore, the ostiole — fig, peepal, banyan).

Flower

The flower is a modified shoot for sexual reproduction. On the thalamus (receptacle) sit four whorls: calyx (sepals) and corolla (petals) are the accessory whorls; androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels) are the essential whorls.

When calyx and corolla look alike they are called a perianth of tepals (lily, onion).

Term Meaning Examples
Actinomorphic ⊕ can be cut into equal halves in any vertical plane mustard, Datura, chilli
Zygomorphic % only one plane gives equal halves pea, bean, gulmohur, Cassia
Monoecious / dioecious male and female flowers on one plant / on separate plants maize, cucurbits / papaya, date palm
Hypogynous (superior ovary) other whorls arise below the ovary mustard, China rose, brinjal
Perigynous (half-inferior) other whorls on the rim of a cup-shaped thalamus plum, rose, peach
Epigynous (inferior ovary) thalamus fuses with the ovary wall; other whorls above it guava, cucumber, sunflower ray florets, apple

Aestivation (arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud): valvate — margins only touch (Calotropis); twisted — each overlaps the next (China rose, cotton, lady's finger); imbricate — irregular overlapping (Cassia, gulmohur); vexillary (descending imbricate) — the large standard covers the two wings, which cover the keel (pea, bean).

Androecium term Meaning Example
Monadelphous filaments united into one bundle China rose (Hibiscus)
Diadelphous two bundles pea, (9) + 1
Polyadelphous more than two bundles Citrus, castor
Syngenesious anthers united, filaments free sunflower (Asteraceae)
Epipetalous stamens attached to petals brinjal, Datura (Solanaceae)
Epiphyllous stamens attached to the perianth lily
Didynamous 4 stamens, 2 long + 2 short tulasi (Lamiaceae)
Tetradynamous 6 stamens, 4 long + 2 short mustard (Brassicaceae)

Gynoecium. Carpels free (apocarpous — lotus, rose, Michelia) or fused (syncarpous — mustard, tomato). Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary:

Marginal — along one suture of a single carpel (pea, legumes). Axile — on the central axis of a multilocular ovary (tomato, China rose, lemon, Liliaceae).

Parietal — on the ovary wall of a unilocular ovary (cucumber, Argemone; mustard, where a false septum, the replum, later divides it). Free central — on a central column with no septa (Dianthus, Primula).

Basal — one ovule at the base (sunflower, marigold).

Fruit

A fruit is a ripened ovary. A true fruit develops from the ovary alone (mango, tomato); a false fruit has other parts too — the thalamus in apple and pear (pome), strawberry and cashew.

A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic (seedless banana, pineapple).

Kind Definition Examples
Simple fruit from one ovary of one flower mango, tomato, pea
Aggregate (etaerio) from many free carpels of one flower strawberry, custard apple (Annona), raspberry, lotus
Composite (multiple) from a whole inflorescence jackfruit and pineapple (sorosis), mulberry (sorosis), fig (syconus)
Simple fruit Type Examples
Legume (pod) dry, monocarpellary, splits along both sutures pea, bean, gram
Siliqua / silicula dry, bicarpellary, long / short, splits from below leaving the replum mustard / Capsella
Capsule dry, multicarpellary, splits by many valves cotton, lady's finger, Datura
Caryopsis dry, one seed, seed coat fused with fruit wall wheat, rice, maize
Cypsela dry, one seed, from inferior ovary, often with pappus sunflower, marigold
Nut dry, hard, one-seeded litchi, cashew
Drupe fleshy; stony endocarp mango, plum, coconut (fibrous mesocarp)
Berry fleshy throughout, many seeds tomato, brinjal, chilli, grape, banana, guava
Hesperidium berry with juicy hairs from the endocarp orange, lemon
Pome false fruit; fleshy thalamus apple, pear
Pepo berry from an inferior ovary, hard rind cucumber, pumpkin

5.2 Brassicaceae, Solanaceae, Fabaceae and Liliaceae

Writing a floral formula

Br = bracteate, Ebr = ebracteate; ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic; ⚥ bisexual, ♂ male, ♀ female; K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium.

The number after the letter is the number of members; brackets mean the members are united; + separates whorls or groups.

A line under G means a superior ovary, a line over it an inferior ovary — in this book the ovary position is written in words. All four families below have a superior ovary (hypogynous flowers).

Character Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) Fabaceae (Papilionaceae) Solanaceae Liliaceae
Habit herbs, pungent juice herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers; root nodules herbs, shrubs; rich in alkaloids monocot herbs with bulbs, rhizomes or corms
Leaves simple, alternate, exstipulate pinnately compound, stipulate, pulvinate base; leaflets may be tendrils simple, alternate, exstipulate mostly basal, linear, parallel venation
Inflorescence raceme (corymbose raceme) raceme solitary or axillary cymes raceme, spike or umbellate cyme (onion)
Flower ebracteate, ⊕, ⚥, tetramerous bracteate, %, ⚥, pentamerous ⊕, ⚥, pentamerous bracteate, ⊕, ⚥, trimerous
Calyx 4, free, in two whorls (2 + 2) 5, united, odd sepal anterior 5, united, persistent —
Corolla 4, free, cruciform (cross-shaped, clawed) 5, papilionaceous: 1 standard, 2 wings, 2 united keel petals; vexillary 5, united, rotate or funnel-shaped, valvate perianth of 6 tepals in two whorls (3 + 3), free or united, petaloid
Androecium 6, tetradynamous (2 short outer + 4 long inner) 10, diadelphous (9) + 1 5, epipetalous, alternate with the petals 6 in two whorls (3 + 3), epiphyllous
Gynoecium bicarpellary, syncarpous; parietal placentation; unilocular, made bilocular by the replum monocarpellary, unilocular, marginal placentation bicarpellary, syncarpous, ovary oblique (septum at 45°); bilocular; axile, swollen placentae tricarpellary, syncarpous, trilocular, axile
Fruit siliqua or silicula legume (pod) berry (tomato, brinjal, chilli) or capsule (Datura, tobacco) capsule (berry in Asparagus)
Seed non-endospermic non-endospermic endospermic endospermic
Floral formula Ebr ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G₍₂₎ Br % ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G₁ ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎ (stamens epipetalous) Br ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎ — P₍₃₊₃₎ when the tepals are united (onion)
Diagnostic character cruciform corolla + tetradynamous stamens + siliqua papilionaceous corolla + diadelphous stamens + legume epipetalous stamens + oblique bicarpellary ovary trimerous perianth (3 + 3) + six stamens + trilocular ovary

Traps in the family questions
  • Tetradynamous (6: 4 long + 2 short) is Brassicaceae; didynamous (4: 2 long + 2 short) is Lamiaceae (tulasi). Do not swap them.
  • In Fabaceae the standard is posterior and the keel anterior; the free stamen is the one opposite the standard. The odd sepal is anterior — the reverse of most families.
  • The Solanaceae ovary is oblique — its septum lies at 45° to the median plane — and the placentae are swollen. The calyx is persistent on the fruit (brinjal, tomato) and enlarges into a bladder in Physalis.
  • Liliaceae is the only monocot of the four; "perianth" (not calyx and corolla) and the number three identify it. Modern classification moves onion and garlic to Amaryllidaceae and Aloe and Asparagus to other families, but the entrance syllabus keeps them in Liliaceae.
  • Pea, gram and lentil are Fabaceae, but this family has two older names — Papilionaceae and Leguminosae; mustard's old family name is Cruciferae.
Family Food and other crops Medicines, drugs, others
Brassicaceae mustard and rapeseed oil (Brassica campestris — tori; B. juncea — rayo saag); cabbage, cauliflower, knol-khol, broccoli (varieties of B. oleracea); radish; turnip Arabidopsis thaliana, the model plant of genetics; Capsella (shepherd's purse), a weed; Iberis (candytuft), ornamental
Fabaceae pulses — lentil (masuro), chickpea (chana), black gram (maas), pigeon pea (rahar), soybean (bhatmas), pea; groundnut timber — sisau (Dalbergia sissoo); green manure (Sesbania, dhaincha); fodder (clover, lucerne); indigo dye; Abrus; root nodules enrich soil
Solanaceae potato (Solanum tuberosum), tomato, brinjal (S. melongena), chilli and capsicum (Capsicum) tobacco (Nicotiana, nicotine); Datura (hyoscine, also called scopolamine; atropine); Atropa belladonna (atropine, dilates the pupil); Withania (ashwagandha); Petunia, ornamental
Liliaceae onion (Allium cepa), garlic (A. sativum), Asparagus racemosus (kurilo, also medicinal) Aloe vera (ghiukumari; burns, skin); colchicine from Colchicum and Gloriosa (induces polyploidy, treats gout); Smilax (sarsaparilla); lilies and tulips, ornamental

5.3 Economic importance of plant groups in Nepal

Group Useful Harmful
Viruses vaccines (attenuated viruses); bacteriophages for phage therapy and as cloning vectors (λ, M13); nuclear polyhedrosis virus (baculovirus) as a biopesticide plant diseases — tobacco mosaic, citrus tristeza (one cause of the decline of Nepal's mandarin orchards), potato leaf roll, bunchy top of banana, yellow vein mosaic of okra, rice tungro; human diseases — polio, rabies, measles, hepatitis, HIV/AIDS, influenza, dengue, COVID-19; foot-and-mouth disease and bird flu of livestock
Bacteria nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium in legumes; free-living Azotobacter, Clostridium); nitrification; decomposition and biogas (methanogens in gobar-gas plants); curd (dahi) by Lactobacillus; Nepali fermented foods — gundruk (lactic acid bacteria in leafy greens) and kinema (soybean fermented by Bacillus subtilis); vinegar (Acetobacter); antibiotics from Streptomyces (streptomycin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol); retting of jute fibre; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin; E. coli making human insulin; Agrobacterium in genetic engineering human diseases — typhoid, cholera, tuberculosis, leprosy, pneumonia, tetanus, diphtheria; plant diseases — bacterial wilt of potato and tomato (Ralstonia), bacterial blight of rice and citrus canker (Xanthomonas), crown gall (Agrobacterium), black rot of crucifers; food poisoning (Clostridium botulinum); denitrification lowers soil fertility
Blue-green algae nitrogen fixation in rice fields (Anabaena, Nostoc, Aulosira, Tolypothrix); Azolla–Anabaena biofertiliser; Spirulina as protein-rich food (single-cell protein); reclaiming alkaline soils toxic water blooms (Microcystis, Anabaena) that kill fish and taint drinking water
Fungi mushrooms — oyster (Pleurotus, the most widely grown in Nepal), button (Agaricus), shiitake; wild morels (Morchella, guchchi chyau, a high-value export); yeast for bread, beer, jaand and raksi (murcha starter); penicillin (Penicillium notatum, Fleming, 1928), griseofulvin, cephalosporin; citric acid (Aspergillus niger); cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum, used in organ transplants); statins (Monascus purpureus); ergot alkaloids (Claviceps); gibberellin (Gibberella fujikuroi); Trichoderma as a biocontrol agent; mycorrhizae; yarsagumba crop diseases — late blight of potato (Phytophthora), rice blast, rusts and smuts of wheat, white rust of mustard; aflatoxin (Aspergillus flavus) in stored maize and groundnut (liver cancer); poisonous mushrooms (Amanita) — deaths every monsoon in Nepal; ringworm and athlete's foot; candidiasis; rotting of timber and food
Algae food (Porphyra, Laminaria, Ulva, Chlorella); agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) for culture media, jellies, ice cream; algin (Laminaria) and carrageenan (Chondrus) as thickeners; iodine and potash from kelps; oxygen and food for every pond and lake; Chlorella in space research water blooms; red rust of tea caused by the parasitic green alga Cephaleuros; slimy growth clogs water tanks
Bryophytes pioneers of succession on rock (after lichens); bind soil and prevent erosion on slopes; peat (Sphagnum) as fuel and potting medium; Sphagnum as packing material and absorbent dressing because it holds many times its weight of water; moss for decoration few; some grow as weeds in nurseries
Pteridophytes niuro (Diplazium esculentum) and Marsilea as vegetables; Azolla biofertiliser; Dryopteris rhizome (filicin, a vermifuge for tapeworm); Lycopodium spores (dusting powder, coating pills); Equisetum (silica, scouring); ornamental ferns (Adiantum, Nephrolepis); fossil ferns formed coal in the Carboniferous bracken (Pteridium) is a weed poisonous to cattle; Salvinia chokes ponds
Gymnosperms timber — chir pine (Pinus roxburghii), blue pine (P. wallichiana), deodar (Cedrus), fir (Abies), spruce; resin tapped from chir pine → rosin and turpentine; taxol (Taxus wallichiana, Himalayan yew) against cancer; ephedrine (Ephedra, trans-Himalaya) for asthma; dhupi (Juniperus) burnt as incense; Cycas (sago), ornamentals (Thuja, Araucaria); paper pulp pine pollen allergy; pine needle litter feeds forest fires
Angiosperms cereals — rice, maize, wheat, millet (kodo), barley; buckwheat (phapar); pulses and oilseeds (mustard, soybean, sesame); vegetables; fruits (mandarin orange — suntala, apple, banana, mango); spices — large cardamom (alaichi, Nepal is the world's leading producer), ginger, turmeric, timur, cinnamon leaf (tejpat); beverages — tea (Ilam), coffee; fibres — jute, cotton, lokta (Daphne, for handmade Nepali paper), allo (Girardinia, nettle fibre); timber — sal (Shorea robusta), sisau, khayer (Acacia catechu, katha), uttis (Alnus nepalensis); medicinal plants (§5.4, chiraito, jatamansi, kutki, satuwa); rudraksha beads; rhododendron (lali gurans, national flower) and orchids invasive weeds — Mikania micrantha (banmara, in Chitwan National Park), Ageratina (kalo banmara), Chromolaena, Lantana, Parthenium (allergy), water hyacinth (Eichhornia) in lakes; parasites — dodder (Cuscuta, akashbeli), mistletoe (Loranthus, ainjeru), Orobanche, Striga; poisonous and narcotic plants — Aconitum (bikh), Datura, Cannabis, opium poppy
Matching questions on economic botany

Most questions pair a product with its source.

Learn these pairs cold: penicillin — Penicillium; streptomycin — Streptomyces; agar — Gelidium; algin — Laminaria; taxol — Taxus; ephedrine — Ephedra; turpentine — Pinus; colchicine — Colchicum; atropine — Atropa; reserpine — Rauwolfia; azadirachtin — neem; eugenol — tulasi; gingerol — ginger; cordycepin — yarsagumba; filicin — Dryopteris; citric acid — Aspergillus niger; kinema — Bacillus subtilis; lokta paper — Daphne.

5.4 Medicinal plants of Nepal: neem, sarpagandha, yarsagumba, tulasi and ginger

Neem Sarpagandha Yarsagumba Tulasi (holy basil) Ginger (aduwa)
Scientific name Azadirachta indica Rauwolfia serpentina (also spelt Rauvolfia) Ophiocordyceps sinensis (formerly Cordyceps sinensis) Ocimum sanctum (= O. tenuiflorum) Zingiber officinale
Family / group Meliaceae (angiosperm tree) Apocynaceae (angiosperm undershrub) Ophiocordycipitaceae — an ascomycete fungus Lamiaceae (angiosperm herb) Zingiberaceae (monocot herb)
Where in Nepal Terai and inner Terai Terai and Siwalik sal forests (now rare; CITES Appendix II) alpine meadows, 3,000–5,000 m (Dolpa, Darchula, Manang, Mustang, Rukum) grown in courtyards everywhere mid-hills (Ilam, Salyan, Palpa, Syangja)
Part used leaves, bark, twigs, seed oil roots the dead larva with the fungal stroma leaves (also seeds, whole plant) rhizome (underground stem)
Active compounds azadirachtin, nimbin, nimbidin reserpine, serpentine, ajmaline cordycepin, cordycepic acid (mannitol), adenosine, polysaccharides eugenol (essential oil), ursolic acid gingerols (fresh), shogaols (dried), zingiberene (aroma)
Main uses antiseptic, antibacterial and antifungal — skin diseases, boils, scabies; twigs as tooth brush (datiwan) for gum health; blood purifier; fever and malaria; seed oil (margosa) for soap and as a spermicide; natural pesticide and neem cake manure high blood pressure (reserpine); sedative and tranquilliser for anxiety, insomnia and mental illness; folk remedy for snake bite and scorpion sting (hence sarpa-gandha) tonic for vigour and stamina, aphrodisiac ("Himalayan Viagra"); kidney and lung disorders; immune booster; anti-fatigue; studied as anti-tumour cough, cold, sore throat, bronchitis, asthma (leaf juice with honey); fever; stress (adaptogen); antibacterial; mosquito repellent; sacred plant indigestion, flatulence (carminative), appetite; nausea and vomiting, motion sickness; cough and cold; anti-inflammatory for joint pain; spice and tea

Notes on each plant

Neem (Azadirachta indica). A large evergreen tree with imparipinnate compound leaves.

Azadirachtin, a limonoid concentrated in the seeds, repels insects and stops them feeding and moulting — the basis of neem biopesticides and neem-coated urea. Leaves are stored with grain and clothes to keep insects away.

Sarpagandha (Rauwolfia serpentina). A small undershrub with whorled leaves and white-pink flowers.

Its root alkaloid reserpine depletes noradrenaline at nerve endings, lowering blood pressure and calming the mind; it was one of the first modern antihypertensive drugs (1950s).

Over-collection for its roots has made it rare in the wild.

Yarsagumba (Ophiocordyceps sinensis). An ascomycete fungus that parasitises the caterpillars of ghost moths (Thitarodes) living in the soil of high alpine meadows.

Spores infect the larva in late summer; the fungus fills and mummifies it during winter (the "winter worm"); in spring a slender, dark, club-shaped stroma grows from the larva's head above the ground (the "summer grass") and bears perithecia with ascospores.

Its Tibetan name, yartsa gunbu, means "summer grass, winter worm".

Collection in May–June is a major cash income for mountain households; the price runs to millions of rupees per kilogram, and over-harvesting has made the species Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.

Tulasi (Ocimum sanctum). An aromatic herb of the mint family with a square stem, opposite decussate leaves, verticillaster inflorescence, bilabiate corolla and didynamous stamens. Its leaf oil is rich in eugenol (also in clove).

It is worshipped in Hindu homes and planted in a tulasi math in the courtyard.

Ginger (Zingiber officinale). A monocot herb whose edible part is a rhizome — a modified underground stem with nodes, scale leaves and buds, not a root.

Fresh ginger owes its pungency to gingerols; on drying (sutho) they turn into the even more pungent shogaols. Nepal is among the world's largest ginger producers and exports much of it to India.

Name traps
  • Yarsagumba is a fungus (Ascomycetes), not a plant or an insect — the "worm" is the dead host larva. Its current genus is Ophiocordyceps.
  • Ginger is a stem (rhizome); sweet potato and carrot are roots.
  • Reserpine is from sarpagandha; azadirachtin is from neem — the two are often swapped in options.
  • Tulasi is in Lamiaceae (didynamous, verticillaster), not Solanaceae.
Reading a floral formula into family and placentation

Problem. A flower is actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous, has 5 fused sepals that persist in the fruit, 5 fused petals, 5 epipetalous stamens, and a bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary with an obliquely placed septum and swollen axile placentation. Name the family.

Solution. Persistent calyx K_{(5)}, epipetalous C_{(5)} A_5, and bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary G_{(2)} with an obliquely placed septum and swollen placenta are diagnostic of Solanaceae (e.g., Solanum nigrum, Datura).

Counting floral parts in Brassicaceae vs Fabaceae

Problem. How many stamens and what arrangement occur in a single flower of(a) Brassica campestris and(b) Pisum sativum?

Solution. Brassica (Brassicaceae) has 6 stamens in a tetradynamous 2 + 4 arrangement (2 outer short, 4 inner long). Pisum (Fabaceae) has 10 stamens in a diadelphous (9) + 1 arrangement (9 fused into a staminal tube, 1 posterior stamen free).

Matching Nepali medicinal plants to active alkaloids and organs used

Problem. Match the active principle and the plant part harvested in Nepal for Rauwolfia serpentina (sarpagandha) and Ophiocordyceps sinensis (yarsagumba).

Solution. Rauwolfia serpentina yields the indole alkaloid reserpine (antihypertensive) from its dried roots.

Ophiocordyceps sinensis is an ascomycete entomopathogenic fungus fruiting from the caterpillar of Thitarodes in alpine meadows (3{,}500\text{–}5{,}000\text{ m}), valued for cordycepin; the whole stroma + mycosed larva is collected.

Chapter summary

  • A modified organ is identified by its origin, not its looks: nodes, buds or scale leaves mean stem (potato, ginger, onion, Colocasia, Opuntia pad, Asparagus cladode, Citrus thorn); sweet potato, carrot and radish are roots; pea tendrils and Opuntia spines are leaves.
  • Racemose inflorescences grow on and open acropetally; cymose ones end in a flower and open basipetally; tulasi has a verticillaster, Euphorbia a cyathium, the fig a hypanthodium and the sunflower a capitulum.
  • Flower terms the paper uses: actinomorphic or zygomorphic; hypo-, peri- or epigynous; valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary aestivation; monadelphous, diadelphous, syngenesious, epipetalous, tetradynamous and didynamous stamens.
  • Placentation is marginal (pea), axile (tomato, lily), parietal (mustard), free central (Dianthus) or basal (sunflower).
  • Fruits are simple, aggregate (many free carpels of one flower) or composite (a whole inflorescence); false fruits such as the apple include the thalamus.
  • Brassicaceae: Ebr ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G₍₂₎, siliqua. Fabaceae: Br % ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G₁, legume. Solanaceae: ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎ with epipetalous stamens and an oblique ovary, berry. Liliaceae: Br ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎, capsule.
  • Every group matters in Nepal: nitrogen-fixing bacteria and blue-green algae, gundruk and kinema, mushrooms and yeast, agar, Sphagnum, Azolla, pine resin and timber, taxol, lokta paper and sal timber — and the harm done by plant viruses, late blight, aflatoxin, poisonous mushrooms and invasive weeds.
  • The five named medicinal plants: neem (Azadirachta indica, azadirachtin), sarpagandha (Rauwolfia serpentina, reserpine, roots), yarsagumba (Ophiocordyceps sinensis, an ascomycete on ghost-moth larvae, cordycepin), tulasi (Ocimum sanctum, eugenol, leaves) and ginger (Zingiber officinale, rhizome, gingerols).

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — Banyan's prop roots hang from horizontal branches like pillars. Maize has stilt roots from the lower nodes; Rhizophora has pneumatophores; carrot is a storage tap root.

2. (c) — The potato is a stem tuber: its "eyes" are nodes with axillary buds. Sweet potato is a tuberous root.

3. (b) — Opuntia spines are modified leaves (its green pad is the stem); pea tendrils are modified terminal leaflets.

4. (d) — A phylloclade has many nodes and internodes. A cladode is only one internode long (Asparagus); a phyllode is a flattened petiole.

5. (b) — Racemose = indefinite growth with acropetal succession. Option (a) describes a cyme; (c) and (d) are cyathium and hypanthodium.

6. (a) — Tulasi (Lamiaceae) has a pair of small cymes at each node that look like a whorl — a verticillaster. The cyathium belongs to Euphorbia, the hypanthodium to the fig.

7. (d) — Hypogynous means the other whorls arise below the ovary, so the ovary is superior.

8. (c) — One bundle = monadelphous (Malvaceae). Diadelphous is two bundles (pea); syngenesious means anthers fused (sunflower).

9. (c) — Tomato has ovules on a central axis in a multilocular ovary. Pea is marginal, mustard parietal, sunflower basal.

10. (b) — Many free carpels of one flower give an aggregate fruit (strawberry, custard apple). A composite fruit comes from a whole inflorescence.

11. (a) — Each develops from an entire inflorescence (sorosis). Aggregate fruits come from a single flower.

12. (d) — Six stamens, four long and two short = tetradynamous. Didynamous (four: two long, two short) belongs to Lamiaceae.

13. (d) — The siliqua is a long bicarpellary pod that splits from below, leaving the seeds on the replum. A legume is the fruit of Fabaceae.

14.(a) — The papilionaceous corolla has one posterior standard, two lateral wings and two anterior petals fused into the keel. Option(b) is cruciform (mustard).

15. (c) — The Solanaceae ovary is bicarpellary with its septum oblique and the placentae swollen. Option (d), with a replum, is Brassicaceae.

16. (b) — A perianth of 3 + 3 tepals, six stamens and a tricarpellary ovary describe the trimerous monocot family Liliaceae.

17. (a) — Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is Solanaceae; mustard is Brassicaceae, pea Fabaceae, onion Liliaceae.

18. (d) — Colchicine comes from Colchicum autumnale and Gloriosa superba, placed in Liliaceae in this course; it blocks spindle formation and doubles chromosome sets.

19. (b) — Kinema is soybean fermented by Bacillus subtilis. Lactobacillus makes curd and gundruk sour; Acetobacter makes vinegar.

20. (c) — Cephaleuros is one of the few parasitic algae; it forms rusty patches on tea leaves. Puccinia causes rust of wheat.

21. (b) — Lokta (Daphne bholua, D. papyracea) bark fibre makes the strong handmade Nepali paper. Sal and sisau are timber trees; uttis is an N-fixing alder.

22. (d) — Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium notatum in 1928. Streptomyces griseus gives streptomycin.

23. (a) — Sarpagandha is Rauwolfia serpentina; the other three are neem, tulasi and ginger.

24. (c) — The fungus parasitises and mummifies ghost-moth caterpillars in the soil of meadows at 3,000–5,000 m; its stroma grows from the larva's head.

25. (d) — Reserpine from sarpagandha roots lowers blood pressure. Azadirachtin is neem's, eugenol tulasi's, gingerol ginger's.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — Stems carry nodes, buds and scale leaves (the potato's eyes); the sweet potato tuber has none, so it is a swollen adventitious root. Storage and position do not decide the organ.

2. (d) — Both protect the plant, but the thorn is a modified branch and the spine a modified leaf: same function, different origin = analogous.

3. (a) — The true leaves of Asparagus are tiny scales; in their axils arise green cladodes, each one internode long. A phyllode is a flattened petiole (Acacia).

4. (c) — The flat disc at the base of the bulb is the true stem; the onion layers are fleshy leaf bases. Growing underground or storing food does not make an organ a stem.

5. (a) — The capitulum has outer ray florets and inner disc florets on a flattened receptacle, ringed by an involucre of bracts. Each "petal" is a ray floret.

6. (b) — Vexillary (descending imbricate) aestivation is the mark of the papilionaceous corolla.

7. (d) — Brassicaceae ovaries have parietal placentation; a false septum (replum) grows across between the two placentae.

8. (c) — Epipetalous stamens have their filaments fused to the corolla tube. Stamens attached to tepals are epiphyllous (lily).

9. (b) — Only Fabaceae has a single carpel with ovules along one margin. The other three have superior ovaries and bisexual flowers too, and Solanaceae also has five sepals.

10. (a) — Trimerous flowers with an undifferentiated perianth are typical monocot features. A superior ovary, bisexuality and axile placentation also occur in dicots.

11. (d) — Rhizobium fixes N₂ in legume nodules; Anabaena fixes it in rice fields and inside Azolla. Both reduce the need for urea.

12. (c) — Gundruk is made by natural lactic acid fermentation (Lactobacillus, Pediococcus), which also preserves the greens. No alcohol or vinegar is involved.

13. (a) — Azadirachtin is an antifeedant and insect growth regulator. It is not an antibiotic for humans and does not fix nitrogen.

14. (c) — Gingerols give fresh ginger its bite; drying converts them to shogaols. Eugenol is tulasi's oil; reserpine and cordycepin belong to sarpagandha and yarsagumba.

15. (b) — Sphagnum holds many times its weight of water, so it is used for packing and as dressings, and it accumulates into peat used as fuel. It has no timber or fruit.

Answers and explanations — Set C

1. (c) — Five united sepals and petals, five stamens and an oblique bicarpellary ovary is Solanaceae. The formula cannot show epipetaly, but the oblique ovary settles it.

2. (a) — Cruciform corolla, tetradynamous stamens and siliqua are the three marks of Brassicaceae — mustard, radish, cabbage.

3. (d) — Standard, wings and keel with (9) + 1 stamens mean Fabaceae, whose monocarpellary ovary ripens into a legume (pod).

4. (b) — A fruit with non-ovarian tissue (the thalamus) is a false fruit; in apple and pear it is a pome. It comes from one flower with one ovary, so it is neither aggregate nor composite.

5. (a) — Trimerous perianth (3 + 3), six stamens and a trilocular superior ovary: onion, which the entrance syllabus keeps in Liliaceae.

6. (c) — Resin tapped from chir pine is distilled into turpentine and rosin. Taxol is from Taxus, agar from Gelidium, penicillin from Penicillium.

7. (d) — Reserpine from the roots of sarpagandha lowers blood pressure; the plant's name ("snake-smell") recalls its folk use for snake bite.

8. (b) — The stalk is the stroma of Ophiocordyceps sinensis, which bears perithecia with asci; the larva is the dead host filled with fungal mycelium.

9. (d) — Neem twigs are stems, tulasi is used for its leaves, and ginger's rhizome is an underground stem.

10. (a) — Sessile flowers in acropetal order on an elongated axis make a spike. A raceme has stalked flowers; a cyme has the oldest flower at the tip.

Model answer D1: Brassicaceae, Fabaceae and Solanaceae (10 marks)

Introduction. Angiosperms are classified into dicots (two cotyledons, net venation, tap root, tetramerous or pentamerous flowers) and monocots (one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots, trimerous flowers). Families are recognised by floral characters.

Leaf simple, alternate compound, with stipules simple, alternate
Inflorescence raceme raceme cymose
Flower actinomorphic, bisexual zygomorphic, bisexual actinomorphic, bisexual
Calyx 4 sepals, free 5, gamosepalous 5, gamosepalous, persistent
Corolla 4 petals in a cross 5: standard, 2 wings, 2 keel (vexillary) 5, gamopetalous
Androecium 6, tetradynamous (4 long + 2 short) 10, diadelphous (9 + 1) 5, epipetalous

(The superior ovary is the hypogynous condition in all three.)

Economic importance.

  1. Brassicaceae: vegetables (cabbage, cauliflower, radish, turnip), oil (mustard, rapeseed, a staple oilseed in Nepal's Terai), ornamentals (candytuft) and a weed (shepherd's purse). Arabidopsis is the model plant of genetics.
  2. Fabaceae: pulses (lentil, soyabean, gram, pea), fodder (clover, alfalfa), timber (Dalbergia, or sisau), dye (indigo), medicine (Glycyrrhiza, liquorice) and green manure (Sesbania). Root nodules with Rhizobium fix nitrogen.
  3. Solanaceae: food (potato, tomato, brinjal, chilli), drug plants (Atropa belladonna giving atropine, Datura, tobacco) and ornamentals (petunia).

Numerical. For a tetradynamous flower the stamens number 2 + 4 = 6 and the petals are 4, so the ratio of stamens to petals is 1.5. A legume pod with 8 seeds, and a plant with 25 pods, gives 200 seeds.

Conclusion. Family identification rests on a few constant floral characters, and each of these three families is of high economic value.

Model answer D2: economic botany (10 marks)

Introduction. Economic botany is the study of plants of use to man for food, fibre, fuel, medicine, shelter and industry.

Food plants.

  1. Cereals (Poaceae) are the staple: rice (Oryza sativa, the main crop of the Terai), wheat, maize, millet (kodo) and barley, rich in starch.
  2. Pulses (Fabaceae) are protein-rich (lentil, black gram, soyabean) and enrich the soil.
  3. Oilseeds: mustard, sesame, groundnut and sunflower.
  4. Sugar: sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) and sugar beet.
  5. Fruits and vegetables give vitamins and minerals, and beverages are tea (Camellia sinensis, grown in Ilam) and coffee (Coffea arabica, grown in Gulmi and Lalitpur).

Fibre plants. Cotton (seed hairs), jute (stem fibre of Corchorus, grown in the Terai), hemp and flax, lokta (Daphne), whose bark gives the traditional Nepali paper, and coir (coconut fruit).

Spices. Large cardamom (Amomum subulatum, Ilam, a major export of Nepal), turmeric, ginger, black pepper, cloves and chilli.

Medicinal plants of Nepal.

Plant Part Use
Rauvolfia serpentina (sarpagandha) root reserpine for high blood pressure
Ophiocordyceps sinensis (yarsagumba) fungus on caterpillar tonic, high value
Azadirachta indica (neem) leaf, bark antiseptic, insecticide
Ocimum sanctum (tulsi) leaf cough, cold
Taxus wallichiana (Himalayan yew) bark taxol, anticancer
Swertia chirayita (chiraito) whole plant fever, digestion
Aloe vera leaf skin care

Conservation. Over-collection of Himalayan herbs threatens species, so CITES, community forestry and cultivation help. The Department of Plant Resources in Kathmandu and national parks conserve medicinal plants.

Other products. Timber (sal, Shorea robusta), rubber (Hevea), resin, tannins and the bio-fuel crop jatropha.

Numerical. If a hectare of rice gives 4\ \text{t} of paddy, which gives 65\% rice on milling, then it yields 2.6\ \text{t} of rice.

A country of 30 million people eating 0.4\ \text{kg} of cereal per person per day needs 12\,000\ \text{t} per day, or about 4.4 million tonnes per year.

Conclusion. Cereals, pulses and oilseeds feed the people, fibres and spices bring income, and Nepal's medicinal plants need careful conservation.
